Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No evidence found of digital case management, incident reporting, or record-keeping systems in Sudanese police stations, including rural ones. Extensive searches across US State Dept human rights reports, UK CPIN, UNODC, police websites (moi.gov.sd, sudanpolice.net), and queries on police IT systems yielded no mentions of digital tools for core police functions like case files or complaints. Police operations described involve manual detention procedures (e.g., 24-hour holds) and physical abuse for confessions, consistent with paper-based processes typical in low-resource African contexts. Ongoing conflict has disrupted infrastructure, but pre-conflict reports (e.g., Afrobarometer) highlight police unprofessionalism without digital references. Official sites show some e-services (vehicle lookup), but not operational records. Rural facilities likely rely entirely on paper, as no digitization pilots or systems noted.

revision_notes: Original cited sources (state.gov, UK CPIN, moi.gov.sd, sudanpolice.net, Afrobarometer) were checked and remain relevant; moi.gov.sd and sudanpolice.net offer only limited public e-services (e.g. vehicle look-up), with no evidence of case-management digitisation. A fresh search surfaced a February 2025 study of information systems within North Kordofan State Police (El Obeid), which confirms the existence of administrative information systems at a state-capital level but does not evidence digital data capture at rural stations, and is not itself an authoritative confirmation of rural facility status. No authoritative source describing digital record-keeping in rural Sudanese police stations was found; the civil war since April 2023 has further degraded state capacity across much of rural Sudan. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Sudan continue to rely entirely on paper-based record-keeping for case files, incident reports and detention logs. No evidence exists of digital case management or record-keeping systems at rural facilities; official police portals (moi.gov.sd, sudanpolice.net) offer limited public e-services such as vehicle look-up but do not extend to operational case data. A 2025 study of administrative information systems in North Kordofan State Police relates to a state-capital administrative unit rather than rural stations, and does not evidence facility-level digitisation. Human rights and security reporting describe manual, paper-based detention and case-handling procedures. The ongoing civil war since April 2023 has further disrupted infrastructure and state capacity across much of rural Sudan, making near-term digitisation of rural police record-keeping unlikely.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Sudan predominantly use paper-based processes for birth registration at point-of-service. Parents or health workers submit paper notices of birth (from hospitals or midwives for home births, common in rural areas) to local civil registry centers, where events are recorded manually before electronic transmission to regional and central databases. The 2011 Civil Registration Act and electronic civil registry enable national digital aggregation with biometrics and national ID numbers, but rural point-of-service remains paper-default, as evidenced by 2012 CRC4D report calling for ICT replacement of paper systems and 2023 Landinfo report noting lower coverage in rural/peripheral areas (<50% in Darfur vs. urban 89%). Mobile units aided mass registration including remote areas, but no evidence of routine digital tools (e.g., tablets, real-time entry) at most rural facilities; ECA report confirms electronic transmission from local but not full district-wide digital business processes. Recent plans like SudaPass (2025) indicate ambition but not rural implementation. Barriers: low density requiring 23k offices, conflict/insecurity (Darfur, Kordofan), poverty, distance, poor infrastructure, home births. National policy aims for digital population register, but rural reality lags with paper at facilities and aggregation higher up.

revision_notes: The Landinfo report (fetched and read in full) describes Sudan's civil registry as centralised, electronic and biometric since the 2011 Civil Registration Act, with registration offices - reached via more than 1,000 mobile units specifically deployed to extend coverage to rural populations - required to capture applicants' fingerprints and photograph electronically at the point of registration for the national identity number underpinning ID cards and passports. This is genuine digital data capture at facility level for the ID/civil-registration function, not merely later digitisation of paper records, which the original score of 1 (Entirely paper) did not credit. Birth notification itself, however, remains paper-based (a paper 'notice of birth' from hospital or midwife) before being brought to a registry office, and rural/peripheral coverage (e.g. Darfur, under 50%) lags urban areas (89%) per Landinfo/MICS data. On balance this supports 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) rather than 1. The Landinfo evidence describes the pre-war system (as of 2021-2023); the civil war since April 2023 has disrupted registration infrastructure in conflict-affected states, so current practice may have degraded from this baseline. Given this genuine uncertainty about whether the promotion holds under current wartime conditions, this row is flagged for human review rather than asserted with confidence.
revised_comments: Digital data capture at rural civil registry offices in Sudan is mixed. For national identity registration, the centralised, biometric civil registry established under the 2011 Civil Registration Act requires applicants to have their fingerprints and photograph captured electronically at the point of registration, with more than 1,000 mobile registration units historically deployed to extend this service to rural areas. Birth registration, by contrast, typically begins with a paper notice of birth issued by a hospital or midwife, which parents must bring to a registry office before an electronic record and certificate are produced; rural and peripheral areas such as Darfur show markedly lower registration coverage than urban centres. Registry offices therefore combine paper-originated notification with subsequent electronic biometric capture and central-database entry, consistent with a mostly-paper, partly-digital process. The civil war since April 2023 has disrupted registration services and infrastructure across much of the country, particularly in conflict-affected states, which may have reduced the digital component of this process below its pre-war baseline.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Sudan predominantly use paper-based systems for recording attendance, enrollment, and grades. EMIS operates at an 'emerging' stage per SABER, centrally coordinated with minimal school-level digital exchange; data lags 12-14 months, implying manual collection at facilities and later aggregation. Only ~50% primary schools have electricity, rare internet/computers in rural areas (66% population rural). UNESCO review notes outdated yearly books (paper-implied) and rapid paper surveys; no evidence of digital tools at rural school level. World Bank highlights EMIS strengthening needs, low ICT readiness. Pilots/digital aggregate reporting do not reach facility recording.

revision_notes: Original UNESCO 2018 review and SABER-ICT study confirmed on re-reading: Sudan's EMIS remains rated at 'emergence level', centrally coordinated with minimal data exchange to individual schools, implying facility-level recording is manual. Fresh 2025 GPE documents confirm the 2023 conflict closed nearly 13,000 schools, disrupted the already paper-reliant, low-tech education system, and that a Transitional Education Plan (2025-2027) and an EMIS-strengthening/digital-mapping project (creating school-location shapefiles for approximately 26,000 schools) remain in early implementation as of 2025, with digital tools not yet reaching classroom-level data capture in rural schools. No evidence found of digital attendance, enrolment or grading capture at the rural school-facility level. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Sudan continue to record attendance, enrolment and grades on paper. The national Education Management Information System operates at an emerging level, coordinated centrally by the Ministry of Education with minimal digital exchange of data with individual schools, and pre-war data lagged by 12-14 months, implying facility-level records are compiled manually before aggregation. The conflict since April 2023 closed nearly 13,000 schools and left the great majority of school-age children out of formal education by 2025, further setting back any digitisation efforts. A Transitional Education Plan (2025-2027) and an EMIS-strengthening initiative, including digital mapping and shapefile creation for around 26,000 schools, are underway but remain at the planning, mapping and pilot stage, and have not yet introduced digital data capture tools at the rural school level. Limited electricity and internet access in rural areas (around 39% rural electrification) further constrain any facility-level digitisation.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Sudan predominantly use paper-based registers and forms for patient data recording at point of service, with 11-13 monthly reporting forms per facility burdening health workers where no statisticians are present. Aggregate data is manually compiled on paper/Excel at facilities, submitted to locality offices, and entered into national DHIS2 at state/locality levels (76% locality coverage, 64% facility reporting rate as of 2020, lower in rural/fragile states). No evidence of widespread EMR or DHIS2 use at rural clinics for individual patient records; digital systems limited to aggregate HMIS reporting upward.WHO EMRO HIS Assessment 2020 Recent pilots include mobile telemedicine (2025), IConnect telehealth with EMR support rolled out to 400 facilities (from pilot in 6), and a survey claiming 65% EMR adoption in unspecified rural facilities (potentially donor-linked).UNICEF digital innovations; Zenodo survey Key barriers: lack of electricity/internet/IT equipment in rural areas, staffing shortages, conflict/insecurity, parallel vertical paper systems.WHO EMRO HIS Assessment 2020 National ambition for integrated DHIS2 contrasts with rural paper reality, where pilots do not yet represent majority practice amid ongoing war disrupting services (70-80% facilities non-operational in some areas).

revision_notes: Original WHO EMRO HIS Assessment 2020 was checked and remains broadly relevant background on the pre-war DHIS2/HMIS structure. Fresh 2025 sources confirm continuity: a December 2025 study on Sudan's health information system finds full reliance on paper records in most health facilities, with the exception of a very small number of private-sector facilities that use electronic recording limited to basic and financial information, and that DHIS2 routine reporting, post-war, covers only six states (Red Sea, River Nile, Northern, Gedaref, Kassala, partial White Nile/Gezira) - a marked contraction from pre-war coverage. A 2024-2025 pilot (EWARS Mobile) in Darfur shows facility staff first log suspected-disease cases on paper tally sheets before a surveillance officer submits weekly aggregate counts via a mobile app, a hybrid, partly-digital process consistent with 'mostly paper, some digital' at facility level, though this is disease surveillance rather than individual patient records. HeRAMS (2025) monitors facility operational status, not patient-level data capture. No evidence of majority EMR adoption in rural clinics; the earlier-cited 65% EMR adoption claim remains unverified and unconfirmed by more authoritative sources. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Sudan predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data at the point of service. A December 2025 assessment finds that health facilities rely almost entirely on paper records, with only a very small number of largely urban, private-sector facilities using electronic recording, and that the national DHIS2 aggregate reporting system, which operates above facility level, now covers routine data collection in only six states following the disruption caused by the war since April 2023. Facility-level digital activity that does exist tends to be partial and pilot-based: for example, a mobile disease-surveillance tool rolled out across Darfur has clinic staff first record suspected cases on paper tally sheets before a surveillance officer submits weekly aggregated counts electronically. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, damaged or non-operational facilities (an estimated 70-80% non-operational in the worst-affected conflict areas), and workforce displacement. This pattern is consistent with a status of mostly paper-based recording with some limited digital elements.
